newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S. seen backing Canadian command of Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seen backing Canadian command of Zaire force.

text.p: U.S. officials hinted on Tuesday that Washington was likely to approve Canadian leadership of a proposed multinational intervention force to aid starving refugees in eastern Zaire.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali told a news conference in Rome that Canada had agreed to lead a force of troops from more than 12 countries, and he hoped the Security Council would approve a mandate in the next few days.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the United States, a key veto-holding member of the Security Council, had been discussing the issue intensively with Canada in the last two days.
"It's on the table. It's in play. It's something we're actively considering," he told reporters accompanying Secretary of State Warren Christopher to a Bosnia conference in Paris.
He said no decision had yet been made by U.S. President Bill Clinton.
But a senior U.S. official, commenting on a published report that the United States had rejected Canadian leadership of the force, told reporters: "I would lead you in the opposite direction."

The United States has come under heavy pressure, especially from France, to agree to the force, which would aim to help some 1.2 million refugees fleeing fighting between Tutsi rebels and Zaire's army.
French Defence Minister Charles Millon on Tuesday accused Washington of dragging its feet on the issue.

The United States has said a force is needed but, mindful of a U.N. mission to Somalia in 1993 which led to heavy casualties among U.S. and other troops involved, has insisted on seeing full details of the force's mandate and funding.
Boutros-Ghali said in Rome that he hoped that the United States would provide logistical support.
U.S. officials have declined to say whether they would provide logistics or ground troops in the event that Clinton agreed to U.S. participation.

Most of the refugees in eastern Zaire are Rwandan Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 when rebels of the Tutsi minority ousted the Hutu-dominated government which had orchestrated the genocide of hundreds of thousands of Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
